body_markdown:
Human papillomavirus, better known as HPV, is one of the most widespread viruses affecting people around the world. Despite its prevalence, HPV is often surrounded by misunderstanding, particularly when it comes to sexual health, cancer and vaccination.


There are more than 200 known types of HPV. Many are harmless and cause no noticeable symptoms, while others can lead to skin or genital warts. A smaller group of high-risk types can cause changes in cells that may eventually contribute to cancer.


Understanding the virus can help people make informed decisions about vaccination, screening and safer sexual practices.


## What is HPV?


HPV is a group of viruses that can infect the skin and areas such as the genitals, mouth and throat. Most HPV infections do not cause symptoms, and the body's immune system usually clears them naturally.


Some types cause common skin warts, including verrucas. Other strains can cause genital warts. These are generally considered low-risk HPV infections because they are not the types most strongly associated with cancer.


The more serious concern involves persistent infection with certain high-risk strains. HPV types 16 and 18 are among the best-known examples. They can interfere with normal cellular processes and, over time, contribute to the development of several cancers.


Having HPV does not mean someone has cancer. In most cases, an HPV infection will not develop into cancer.


## HPV is linked to more than cervical cancer


Cervical cancer is probably the condition most people associate with HPV, but the virus can also play a role in other cancers.


High-risk HPV infections have been associated with cancers affecting the vulva, vagina, anus, penis and parts of the mouth and throat. This is one reason HPV vaccination is recommended for both boys and girls in vaccination programmes.


The connection between HPV and cancer generally involves persistent infection. When the immune system does not eliminate a high-risk infection, abnormal cellular changes can sometimes develop over a period of years.


Smoking may also increase the risk because it can affect the immune system's ability to deal with HPV infection.


## How does HPV spread?


HPV can be transmitted through intimate skin-to-skin contact. Sexual transmission can occur through vaginal, anal or oral sexual activity, but penetration is not necessarily required.


Because the virus can be present without causing visible symptoms, a person may transmit HPV without knowing they have it.


Genital warts can also be caused by HPV. Removing visible warts does not necessarily mean that the virus has immediately disappeared from the body. The immune system generally needs time to clear the infection.


HPV can also be transmitted through shared sex toys if they are not properly cleaned between users.


## Myth: You can always tell when someone has HPV


One of the biggest misconceptions about HPV is that an infection should be obvious.


In reality, most people with HPV have no symptoms. They may therefore be unaware that they have the virus.


This makes HPV very different from some infections that produce immediate or noticeable symptoms. The absence of genital warts or other visible changes does not prove that HPV is absent.


It also means that an HPV diagnosis should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of recent sexual activity or infidelity. HPV can remain unnoticed for a considerable period, making it difficult to determine when or from whom an infection was acquired.


## Myth: Condoms completely prevent HPV


Condoms remain an important way of reducing the risk of sexually transmitted infections, but they cannot provide complete protection against HPV.


The reason is that HPV can infect areas of skin that are not covered by a condom. Consistent condom use can still reduce exposure, but it should not be considered a guarantee against infection.


Using condoms and avoiding the sharing of sex toys without appropriate cleaning can form part of a broader approach to reducing transmission.


## HPV vaccination is an important form of protection


Vaccination is one of the most effective ways to reduce the risk from the HPV types responsible for many HPV-related cancers and genital warts.


The vaccine is designed to prevent infection with targeted HPV types. It does not treat an HPV infection that someone already has, which is why vaccination is particularly valuable when given before exposure.


HPV vaccination is offered routinely to young people in the UK, with eligibility and catch-up arrangements depending on age and circumstances.


Vaccinating boys as well as girls is important because HPV can affect people of all sexes and can contribute to cancers beyond cervical cancer.


## Myth: Vaccination means cervical screening is unnecessary


HPV vaccination significantly reduces the risk of infection with important high-risk HPV types, but it does not protect against every HPV type that can contribute to cervical cancer.


That is why vaccination and cervical screening serve different purposes.


Cervical screening is designed to identify high-risk HPV and, where necessary, investigate or monitor changes in cervical cells. Detecting these changes early can allow appropriate follow-up before serious disease develops.


Anyone invited for cervical screening should therefore continue to attend even if they have received the HPV vaccine.


## What symptoms should people take seriously?


HPV itself frequently causes no symptoms. However, people should seek medical advice if they experience unusual changes such as unexplained bleeding, bleeding after sex, persistent changes in vaginal discharge or other symptoms that concern them.


These symptoms do not automatically mean cancer. There are many possible causes, including conditions that are not serious. However, persistent or unusual symptoms should not simply be ignored.


People can also speak with a GP or sexual health professional if they are concerned about genital warts, HPV exposure or sexually transmitted infections.


## Why understanding HPV matters


HPV is common, and infection is not something that should automatically carry shame or stigma. Because the virus can be transmitted without symptoms and can remain undetected, an HPV infection does not necessarily indicate when transmission occurred.


The most useful response is informed prevention rather than fear.


Vaccination, appropriate cervical screening, safer sexual practices and awareness of unusual symptoms can all play a role in reducing the health consequences associated with HPV.


For many people, an HPV infection will never cause serious illness. Nevertheless, certain persistent high-risk infections can have significant consequences, which is why prevention and screening remain important.
